newsitem.title: USA: Coffee drinkers may cut back as prices boil over.
newsitem.headline: Coffee drinkers may cut back as prices boil over.

text.p: A run-up in coffee prices to the highest level in two-and-a-half years might make consumers think twice before brewing that second pot, industry analysts say.
Fuelled by lower production in Central and South America and a decline in U.S. inventories to 20-year lows, the wholesale price of unroasted coffee has nearly doubled in the past three months.
On New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, May coffee futures are trading around a lofty $2 a pound, the highest since October, 1994.
In response, leading coffee roasters like Folgers Coffee Co. and Maxwell House have raised their prices by a minimum of 20 percent.
On Monday, Folgers announced its second price hike in a month. Its standard 13-ounce can of coffee priced at $2.21 in February now costs $2.86.
"Anytime coffee prices go up, consumption usually goes down," said Jack Maxwell, who follows the food and beverage industry for Wheat First Securities in Richmond, Va.

The United States is still the world's top coffee-drinking country, but consumption has been in decline for years as Americans increasingly switch to cooler and sweeter beverages like cola and iced tea. The latest rise in coffee prices should accelerate the trend, Maxwell said.

Some coffee drinkers might not think twice before laying out another dime for a double latte that already costs $2 or more. But for the roughly 70 percent of U.S. consumers who still drink their coffee at home, sticker shock is more keenly felt.

"It is reasonable to expect that Americans who love coffee are going to be drinking less coffee in 1998 than in 1996 because it is not going to be economical," said Donald Schoenholt, president of Gillies Coffee, a Brooklyn, N.Y.-based coffee importer and roaster.
"At these prices levels, the ritual of coffee drinking could become luxury and not a habit," he added.

The last time coffee prices neared these levels was in 1994, when a shortage of coffee from top producer Brazil brought about widespread increases at the retail level. Consumers responded by cutting back on coffee drinking, and per capita consumption fell, says Wheat First's Maxwell.
Based on preliminary 1996 figures, Maxwell estimated that Americans drank an average of 20.4 gallons of coffee last year. That compares with 23.4 gallons per capita in 1994, and 26.5 gallons in 1992.
Rather than forgo a second cup at home, Maxwell said, price-sensitive consumers often stretch a can of coffee by adding more water to the pot.
Small, "specialty" roasters, who sell high-end coffee beans to speciality shops as well as supermarkets, are especially vulnerable to the price rise.

Unlike the big supermarket brands, they lack the backing of a large, diversified corporation. Top seller Folgers is owned by consumer products giant Procter & Gamble, while Maxwell House is part of Philip Morris Cos. Inc.'s Kraft Foods division.
"It's going to hurt the speciality sector more because speciality coffee is a one-trick pony," Schoenholt said.
The prospect of weaker demand has caused alarm in some producing countries, where coffee is a vital source of income.
On Monday, producers' representatives, who are more accustomed to lamenting low world prices, took the unusual step of calling a meeting to discuss whether the price jump would hurt demand.
"We don't want (high prices) to hit consumption levels," said Roberio Oliveira Silva, secretary general of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries.
The 14-member cartel, which includes top-growers Brazil and Colombia, set the meeting for later this month.

Whether higher prices at the cash register scare consumers away depends largely on how long the increases last, analysts say. For a short time, some said, the higher prices could even boost demand as consumers rush to stock up on their favourite brand before the price increases take effect.

Both Folgers and Maxwell House announced increases several weeks before they were made official. While the latest Folgers' price change took effect immediately, Maxwell House's increase does not kick in until March 31.
"If anything, Joe coffee-drinker is rushing to the supermarket and hoarding coffee," said Judith Ganes, a commodities analyst at Merrill Lynch. "Consumers are stocking up."
